What interests me about Kaikuvaara beyond the technical overlap is the operational context. At Vireo, a processing fault means a missed radar track on a cargo vessel — undesirable but recoverable. The instrument domain is different: tighter tolerances, harsher operating environments, and data that cannot be recollected if the processing gets it wrong. I have not worked under those constraints, but the engineering discipline they demand is exactly what I want to move toward.

One thing I want to mention that does not fit neatly on a CV: I co-authored a paper on waveform diversity for marine radar that appeared in ISRT Radar, Sonar & Navigation in 2022. It came from a collaboration with a visiting researcher from Kallavesi University of Technology who spent six months at our office. We designed the waveform scheme together, I implemented the processing chain and ran the sea trials, and she wrote the analytical bounds. It is the only published paper I have, but the experience convinced me that I value having work exist somewhere beyond internal documents.

On the language side, my entire career at Vireo has been conducted in English. The team is international — colleagues from Finland, France, India, the UK — and English is the language for all code, specifications, design reviews, test reports, and customer presentations. I have also presented at two SESE radar conferences. English is simply the language I do engineering in.

I am a Finnish citizen and have been in Oulu since 2013. Vireo to Kaikuvaara would be a change of employer without a change of city. I would rather discuss the engineering than restate my CV, so I will leave it there.
